analysis.one_liner: Strips the National Labor Relations Board of its power to prosecute labor-law violations.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so the Board could investigate unfair labor practices but could not prosecute them. The General Counsel would lose the power to issue complaints, the Board could no longer make rules affecting workers' or employers' substantive rights, and enforcement would instead fall to private lawsuits in federal court.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing NLRB complaints over practices like retaliation against union activity benefit most: prosecutions by the Board's General Counsel, which cost workers and unions nothing, would be replaced by civil suits that workers and unions must pay to litigate themselves. Employers would also be shielded from Board rulemaking that creates substantive worker-rights rules, such as posting requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers facing union or Board actions

how_it_helps.text: Removes the General Counsel's authority to issue and prosecute unfair labor practice complaints before the Board, leaving only investigation and a written summary of findings to the parties [S2][S3].
Limits Board rulemaking to the Board's internal functions and bars rules that affect the substantive rights of any employer, employee, or labor organization [S2][S3].
Replaces Board-initiated enforcement with private civil actions, including injunctions, brought in federal district court by an aggrieved party [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and unions: the current complaint process is free and handled by a government prosecutor; under this bill a worker claiming an unfair labor practice would have to sue in federal court at their own expense. Any employer wrongly accused would also bear litigation costs without a government screening process.

drawbacks.text: Free, government-prosecuted enforcement would be replaced by civil litigation, which favors parties who can afford lawyers and would make labor-law remedies much harder for individual workers to reach [S2].
Barred from substantive rulemaking, the Board could no longer update worker- and employer-rights rules through the normal regulatory process, leaving the 1935 statute frozen [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's declared purpose of restraining an agency it viewed as overreaching comes at the cost of dismantling the main enforcement mechanism of federal labor law. Because litigation is expensive and slow, the private-suit replacement would function far better for deep-pocketed employers than for the workers it nominally protects.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia introduced the bill on September 20, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 75 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].
No further action followed the referral; the bill never received a markup, floor vote, or companion action in the Senate before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions are better off, since the NLRB's free, government-run complaint and prosecution process was left intact rather than replaced by costly private litigation. Employers facing Board enforcement lost a chance to weaken it.

for.name: Rep. Austin Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 75 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; it died in committee without any recorded votes [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers, especially those facing union organizing or Board complaints
industries.note: The bill removes free government prosecution of unfair labor practices and replaces it with private lawsuits workers must fund, and bars Board rules that create substantive rights. Its value to employers lies in weaker, costlier enforcement of worker protections [S2][S3].

Unions rely on Board prosecution to police employer retaliation and bargaining bad faith; shifting enforcement to expensive private suits raises the cost of using the law. Unions and their members would both bear higher enforcement costs [S2].

The bill strips the agency of its complaint-issuing and rulemaking powers, reducing it to an investigator that passes findings to the parties. Its function as the nation's labor-law enforcer would effectively end [S2][S3].
